newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Sierra Leone coup leaders want rebels in government.
newsitem.headline: Sierra Leone coup leaders want rebels in government.

text.p: Sierra Leone's new military rulers said on Monday they planned to bring rebels of the Revolutionary United Front into the government to consolidate an elusive peace in the country's civil war.
A spokesman for the new Armed Forces Revolutionary Council (AFRC), which toppled the civilian government on Sunday, urged people to return to work.
In central Freetown firefighters battled a blaze at the central bank caused by Sunday's fighting, which gutted the Treasury building. Fifteen bodies were taken to the hospital morgue.
An army major went on state radio on Sunday night to declare himself the new head of state and called on Nigeria to release rebel RUF leader Foday Sankoh to join the new government.

Major Johnny Paul Koromah said he had overthrown President Ahmad Tejan Kabbah because his elected government had failed to consolidate peace and the political situation had encouraged tribal conflict.

"At this moment, attempts are being made to work out modalities for the RUF to join us in order to ensure the peace that has eluded us for so long," AFRC spokesman Paul Thomas said in a radio broadcast on Monday.
Sankoh has been in Nigeria since March and is currently held at a hotel in the capital Abuja. His rebel movement has been fighting successive governments since 1991.

Shops and markets were closed on Monday but hundreds of people came out to view the damage caused by Sunday's fighting around the presidential offices at State House, which were defended by Nigerian troops stationed in Sierra Leone under a regional defence pact.
The new leaders warned against foreign intervention in Sierra Leone's internal affairs.
They asked schools to open to allow children to take examinations, and witnesses said soldiers had been helping take children to school.
Thomas said owners of vehicles commandeered during the coup could come to collect them, and apologised for the inconvenience.

One of the coup leaders' first decrees reflected army grievances against Kabbah, abolishing a civilian militia on which he had come to rely against the rebels in fighting continuing despite a peace accord last year.
The coup drew condemnation from U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan and Organisation of African Unity leader Salim Ahmed Salim. Germany called it a blow for West African democracy.

"The United Nations and the international community firmly uphold the principle that the will of the people shall be the basis of the authority of governments, and that governments, democratically elected shall not be overthrown by force," Annan said, describing himself as "distressed" by the news.
Salim urged African states to condemn Sierra Leone's new leaders and not to welcome them into OAU ranks. The organisation holds a summit in Zimbabwe next week.

Troops stormed Freetown's maximum security prison on Sunday and freed 600 inmates, including soldiers charged with plotting against Kabbah. Sierra Leone's ambassador to the United States, John Leigh, said the soldiers gave arms to their jailed colleagues and common criminals to attack government buildings.

Land borders and air and sea ports were closed until further notice and the capital Freetown spent the night under a curfew imposed after looting of Lebanese-owned businesses, private homes and United Nations offices and residences.
